title: Mercury 2.5 LLM hits 770 tokens per second
content:
Mercury 2.5 Intelligence, Performance & Price Analysis
Model summary
Mercury 2.5 is below average in intelligence, but well priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It's also notably fast and fairly concise. The model supports text input, outputs text, and has a 260k tokens context window.
Mercury 2.5 scores 12 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it below average among comparable models (median: 13). When evaluating the Intelligence Index, it generated 35M tokens, which is fairly concise in comparison to the median of 85M.
Pricing for Mercury 2.5 is $0.25 per 1M input tokens (moderately priced, median: $0.25) and $0.75 per 1M output tokens (moderately priced, median: $0.90). On average, it costs $0.06 per task to evaluate Mercury 2.5 on the Intelligence Index.
At 770 tokens per second, Mercury 2.5 is notably fast (109).
Metrics are compared against models of the same class:
- Non-reasoning models → compared only with other non-reasoning models
- Reasoning models → compared across both reasoning and non-reasoning
- Open weights models → compared only with other open weights models of the same size class:
- Tiny: ≤4B parameters
- Small: 4B–40B parameters
- Medium: 40B–150B parameters
- Large: >150B parameters
- Proprietary models → compared across proprietary and open weights models of the same price range, using a blended 3:1 input/output price ratio:
- <$0.15 per 1M tokens
- $0.15–$1 per 1M tokens
- >$1 per 1M tokens

report.summary: Inception's proprietary Mercury 2.5 reasoning model posts 770 tokens/second output speed with a 260k context window, at below-median intelligence (12 vs. 13) and mid-tier pricing.
report.background: The frontier-model race has largely been about raw intelligence, but a parallel market has emerged around throughput, latency and cost — the metrics that decide whether an agent loop finishes in seconds or minutes. Mercury 2.5 arrives into that second contest. Built by Inception, a lab whose Mercury line has been positioned around extreme generation speed rather than top-tier benchmark scores, the model is a proprietary reasoning system released on September 8, 2026. It is text-only, non-multimodal, and offers a 260k-token context window. On Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index it scores 12 against a median of 13, while outputting at 770.4 tokens/second versus a peer median of 108.6 — roughly seven times faster. Pricing is $0.25 per 1M input and $0.75 per 1M output tokens, a blended $0.14 at a 7:2:1 cache/input/output ratio.
key_points: Speed is the headline, by a wide margin: 770.4 tokens/second versus a median of 108.6 t/s for reasoning models in the same price tier. That is roughly seven times faster than typical peers, making Mercury 2.5 one of the fastest reasoning models currently tracked by Artificial Analysis.

Intelligence is deliberately mid-tier. A score of 12 on the Intelligence Index lands just below the comparable median of 13, so buyers are trading benchmark leadership for throughput. On the full index evaluation it emitted 35M tokens versus a median of 85M — notably concise, which compounds the raw speed advantage into lower end-to-end latency and cost.

Pricing sits at the middle of the market: $0.25 per 1M input tokens (median $0.25) and $0.75 per 1M output tokens (median $0.90). At a blended 7:2:1 cache-hit/input/output ratio that works out to about $0.14 per 1M tokens, and roughly $0.06 to run one Intelligence Index task.

It is proprietary, text-only, and single-provider. Weights are not released, parameter count is undisclosed, and there is no image input — so it cannot replace multimodal or self-hosted models. Availability runs through one API provider (Inception's own API), a concentration risk for production users.

Latency is not uniformly fast: time to first token is 2.91s, slightly worse than the 2.22s peer median. Mercury 2.5 therefore benefits long generations far more than short, snappy single-turn exchanges — an important distinction when speccing it into an application.
report.impact: Mercury 2.5 sharpens a fault line in the AI industry: intelligence per dollar versus tokens per second. Most labs chase benchmark leadership; Inception is betting that for agentic workloads — multi-step tool calls, code agents, document pipelines — throughput and low token verbosity matter more than a single point on a benchmark. For developers, a sevenfold speed advantage with a 260k context window and reasonably priced output tokens makes it attractive for latency-sensitive pipelines where 'good enough' reasoning suffices and retries are cheap. For regular users it means chat and agent experiences that feel near-instant, at the cost of harder questions being answered less reliably than by frontier models. The bigger signal is competitive pressure: if a mid-intelligence model can win on speed, rivals must optimise inference efficiency, not just benchmark scores.
report.tools: Start with Artificial Analysis (artificialanalysis.ai) to track Mercury 2.5 against peers on speed, TTFT, cost and index scores as new providers appear. Try the Inception API directly, or route through OpenRouter or LiteLLM to benchmark it against your current model without rewriting integration code. For agent and coding workloads, test in Cline, Aider or LangGraph pipelines where high output speed compounds over many steps, and use prompt-caching and streaming client libraries to exploit the cheap $0.14 blended rate.
